 1.1 Role of Software

What is software?

 Software (Pressman): (1) instructions (computer programs) that when executed provide desired features, function and
 performance; (2) data structures that enable the programs to adequately manipulate information; (3) descriptive information
 (documentation) that describes the operation and use of the programs.


The lecture also gives the shorter form (Chapter 1.pptx, slide 7): Software = Programs + Documents + User Manual, and
Engineering = systematic, scientific and well-defined processes to produce a good-quality software product. Software controls
phones, banking, medical equipment, aircraft, cars, e-commerce and cloud services, so it is a critical part of almost every industry.

Software engineering principles: Abstraction and Decomposition

 Abstraction hides implementation detail and presents only the essential features of a system, so developers can focus on
 functionality without worrying about internal complexity. Decomposition divides a large system into smaller manageable

Generic vs customised products
(asked in a past paper, not in the lecture files; from Sommerville Ch.1). Generic (shrink-wrapped) products are produced by a
company for the open market and sold to any customer (MS Office, Tally): the developer owns the specification. Customised
(bespoke) products are commissioned by one customer and built to its specification (a hospital system): the customer owns the
specification. Full answer is in the PYQ block at the end of this unit.


 1.3 Legacy Software

 Legacy software is old software, developed decades ago, that is still in use (with modifications) because it performs critical
 business functions. Pressman: 'software that has been inherited from the past and is still in operation because it is essential to
 an organisation'.


 Characteristics: longevity and business criticality; sometimes also poor quality — inextensible designs, convoluted code, test
 cases and results never archived, poorly maintained change history, lack of support and documentation, hard to troubleshoot,
 exposed to security threats.
 Risk: the rapid growth of such systems is a risk to large organisations because they may need outdated hardware and operating
 systems.

 Example (slide 29): government tax systems — income-tax processing, pension management, employee records run for
 decades.

Why legacy software must evolve (U1.pptx slide 12)
 New technology → people want personalised systems; latest software has specifications the old one lacks.

 Not compatible with fast modern systems.
 Must be re-architected to work in a network environment.

 Security issues found daily must be fixed.
 Software is used in every industry (education, health, retail, transport…) so improving it benefits all.

Goal of modern SE: build new systems out of old ones, make them interoperable, secure and more efficient. Legacy software is
treated as necessary but of limited capacity, and is eventually replaced by newer systems.

 PAST PAPER Final 09-Dec-2025 (AY 2025-26) · Q1a · 5 marks

 Q. Explain challenges in maintaining Legacy software.

 Answer.
 Legacy software is old software that is still in use because it performs critical business functions (longevity + business criticality).
 Maintaining it is hard for these reasons:

 Poor design / inextensible architecture — a change in one place breaks others; convoluted code is hard to understand.

 Missing documentation and archived tests — test cases and results were never kept, change history is poorly maintained, so
 the effect of a change cannot be predicted.

 Obsolete technology — needs outdated hardware, operating system and languages; spare parts and skilled developers are
 scarce.

 Security vulnerabilities — unpatched old components expose the system to threats, and new security issues appear every
 day.

 Compatibility / integration — not compatible with modern fast systems, cannot work in a network/cloud environment
 without re-architecture.

 Business risk — the system cannot be switched off (critical), so every change must be done while it keeps running; replacing
 it is costly and risky.

 Changing needs — users want personalised, new-technology features the old system lacks.

 Example: a government income-tax or pension system running for decades. Way out: adapt, enhance, extend or re-architect it
 and make it interoperable with new systems; replace it eventually.

PAST PAPER Final 09-Dec-2024 (AY 2024-25) · Q1a · 5 marks

 Q. How does software deterioration differ from hardware wear? What are the primary factors contributing to deterioration?

 Answer.
 Hardware wear is physical: heat, friction, dust and vibration degrade components, so the failure rate follows the bathtub curve
 — high early (infant mortality), low and steady in useful life, rising again at wear-out. A worn part is replaced by a spare.

 Software deterioration is logical: software has no moving parts and does not wear out, so its idealised failure curve stays flat
 after early defects are fixed. In practice, however, software is changed; each change can introduce new defects (side effects), so
 the failure rate spikes and the minimum level creeps up (actual curve) — the software deteriorates though it never wears. There
 are no spare parts: every failure is a defect that must be corrected by changing the design/code.

 PAST PAPER Final 22-Nov-2022 (AY 2022-23) · Q1a · 5 marks

 Q. “Until the software developer gets the program ‘running’ there is no way of assessing its quality.” True/False with
 justification.

 Answer.
 False. This is the practitioner myth 'quality can be assessed only when the program is running'. In reality quality can be built in
 and measured at every phase: requirements and design can be checked by formal technical reviews/walkthroughs and
 inspections, models can be analysed for completeness and consistency, code can be reviewed or statically analysed before
 execution, and SQA activities/metrics apply throughout. Reviews are in fact one of the most effective ways to find defects early,
 when they are cheapest to fix.

 PAST PAPER Re-Exam 30-Jan-2023 · Q1a · 5 marks

 Q. “Software requirements continually change, but change can be easily accommodated because software is flexible.” True/False
 with justification.

 Answer.
 False (customer myth: 'requirements can be changed anytime because software is flexible'). Software is easier to modify than
 hardware, but the cost of change rises sharply with time: a change at the requirements stage is cheap, in design it costs more,
 in coding more still, and after delivery it needs redesign, re-coding, re-testing and re-documentation, extra resources and
 schedule. Each change may also introduce side-effect defects (deterioration) and break other modules.

 Stage when change is made Relative effort
 Requirements 1×
 Design ≈ 5–10×
 Coding ≈ 10–20×
 After delivery ≈ 50–200× (rule of thumb)


 (The multipliers are illustrative rules of thumb, not lecture figures.) Conclusion: frequent late changes increase development
 time, cost and complexity; manage them through change control and iterative/agile processes rather than assuming they are
 free.

Is the number of loops fixed? No. Each loop is one phase/iteration; the number depends on project size, complexity, risks and

It is not one fixed process but a framework that can incorporate other models (waterfall, prototyping, incremental) loop by loop,
according to risk. Example (Online Banking, Verma): Loop 1 — prototyping to gather requirements; Loop 2 — waterfall to design
the architecture; Loop 3 — incremental model to build account management, fund transfer and loan services.

 Role of the product backlog in managing change: it is a single, prioritised, living list. A new or changed requirement is simply

 update; Retrospective adapts the process; Sprint Planning re-selects the highest-value items every cycle.

 Q. Why is the spiral model considered a meta model?

 Answer.
 A meta model is a model that can contain other models. The spiral model does not prescribe one fixed development process: it
 is a risk-driven framework in which each loop can use a different process model chosen according to the risks of that loop.

 It can incorporate waterfall (systematic design), prototyping (clarify requirements) and incremental (gradual delivery).

 Each loop can follow a different approach based on risk analysis.


 Example — online banking (lecture): Loop 1: prototyping to gather requirements; Loop 2: waterfall to design the
 architecture; Loop 3: incremental model to build account management, fund transfer and loan services.

 3.1 Visual Modeling with UML

 Model = a simplified representation of a real-world system that keeps the important aspects and hides unnecessary detail (a
 blueprint). Visual modeling = representing a software system with graphical diagrams and symbols. UML (Unified Modeling
 Language) = a standard general-purpose graphical language to specify, visualize, construct and document the artifacts of a
 software system; developed by Booch, Jacobson and Rumbaugh at Rational and adopted as a standard by the OMG. UML is a
 modeling language — NOT a programming language and NOT a methodology.


Why we build models: to capture knowledge of a process simply; to communicate desired structure and behaviour; to understand
the system (exposing simplification and reuse); to discover new knowledge such as how two systems will interact. UML helps to
visualise, specify, communicate and document; to understand complex systems part by part; to document decisions. Example (U3
slides 1–3): a real library has students, librarians, books, publishers, shelves, computers, registers, fines…; the model keeps Student
→ Search Book → Issue Book → Return Book → Pay Fine.

 3.4 Use Case Model

 A use case diagram graphically represents the functional requirements of a system: how users (actors) interact with the
 system to achieve specific goals, giving a high-level view from the user's perspective without internal implementation. A use
 case is functionality provided by the system — it describes what the system does for a user, not how. An actor is an object or
 set of objects external to the system that interacts with it to get meaningful work done (human, device or other system — e.g.
 fingerprint scanner/RFID reader in an ATM). The system boundary (subject) is a rectangle enclosing all use cases and
 separating inside from outside.


Why: the use case model lets customer and developer communicate WHAT the system should do — a visual contract between
them, and the basis for design and test cases. Notation: actor = stick figure with name below; use case = ellipse with name inside;
system = rectangle (use cases inside, actors outside); association = line (a use case is triggered by an actor; every actor must be
linked to ≥ 1 use case and every use case to ≥ 1 actor; associations among actors or among use cases are usually not shown).

 3.5 Activity Diagram

 An activity diagram is a behavioural UML diagram that shows the flow of control from activity to activity — the workflow of a
 use case, business process or algorithm, including decisions and parallel flows. It is essentially a flow chart extended with
 concurrency (fork/join) and responsibility (swimlanes). [U3 / N1 / ActivityDiagrams.ppt]


Why use it: model the workflow of a business process or use case, show parallel activities, capture the logic of an operation, and

decision — diamond with one input and several guarded outputs; (6) merge — diamond that re-unites alternative paths; (7) fork
— thick bar splitting one flow into concurrent flows; (8) join — thick bar that waits for ALL incoming flows; (9) note; (10) partition /
swimlane — columns or rows showing WHO performs each activity.

 4.1 Requirement Engineering Tasks

 Requirements Engineering (RE) is the systematic process of identifying, analysing, documenting, validating and managing the
 requirements of a software system. It is the connector between modeling, analysis, design and construction and the
 foundation of planning and implementation. A requirement specifies what the system should do (not how). [N3]


RE process: feasibility study → requirements elicitation → specification → verification/validation → management. RE tasks (the
seven tasks of the lecture): Inception, Elicitation, Elaboration, Negotiation, Specification, Validation, Requirements Management.
The slide deck [N3 pdf] groups the main activities as elicitation, analysis (elaboration), specification and validation, plus negotiation
and review.

 Fig 4.1 — The seven requirement-engineering tasks (changes found later feed back into earlier tasks)


 Task Purpose and key points [N3]
 1 Inception get started: ask basic questions — understand the problem, who wants a solution, nature of the solution,
 communication and collaboration between customer and developer
 2 Elicitation gather requirements from stakeholders using systematic techniques (not just 'what do you want?'). Problems: scope
 (unnecessary detail, ill-defined, impossible), understanding (customer unsure, developer misunderstands), volatility
 (requirements change over time)
 3 Elaboration / refine and expand the gathered requirements; build models (use cases, activity diagrams) and prototypes; check
 Analysis they are clear, complete, consistent, feasible, necessary
 4 Negotiation customer and developer discuss, resolve conflicts, prioritise and agree: availability of resources, delivery time,
 scope, project cost, development estimates; risks are considered so both sides are satisfied
 5 Specification written document, set of models, collection of use cases, prototype → the SRS (Software Requirements
 Specification), in language the customer understands; models: DFD, data dictionary, etc.
 6 Validation formal technical review of the specification: all requirements stated and met, errors corrected, standards followed.
 Techniques: reviews/inspections, prototyping, test-case generation, automated consistency analysis. Team:
 engineers, customers, users, stakeholders
 7 Requirements identify, control, track and manage requirements and their changes during the project (new requirements → analyse
 Management impact, prioritise, decide)

Win-win negotiation
Pressman, Requirements Engineering (negotiation) In win-win negotiation the customer and the developer both give and take
until each party feels it has won: the customer gets a system that satisfies the most important needs, and the developers get
realistic, achievable budgets and deadlines. Steps: identify the key stakeholders → determine each one's 'win conditions' →
negotiate to reconcile them into a set of win-win conditions → agree on the requirements that satisfy them.

 A data flow diagram (also called a bubble chart) is a simple hierarchical graphical model that represents a system in terms of

 Each function is a 'processing station' that consumes input data and produces output data. [N4, DFD]

 Symbol Meaning and rules
 External entity (rectangle) real physical entity that inputs data to / consumes data from the system; also called terminator, source or

 Concept Rule [N4, DFD]

 Asynchronous two bubbles connected through a data store are independent in speed
 Context diagram (Level most abstract DFD: the whole system as one bubble, with the data it inputs/outputs and the external entities
 0)
 Level 1 examine the SRS: each of the 3–7 high-level functions becomes a bubble with its input and output data
 Higher levels each bubble is decomposed ('factored' / 'exploded') into 3 to 7 sub-bubbles: identify the sub-functions and their
 input and output data. Decomposing into only 1–2 bubbles is redundant
 Numbering bubbles are numbered 0, then 0.1…0.n, then 0.3.1… so each parent can be traced
 Principles of structured top-down decomposition; divide and conquer; graphical representation using DFD

 4.5 Control Flow Model

 The control flow model represents how control of the system moves from one operation or activity to another based on
 conditions, decisions, loops and events. It answers: 'In what order are the operations performed, and how does the system
 decide what to do next?' It belongs to the analysis model alongside data modeling, data flow modeling and behavioral
 modeling. [N3 docx]


It shows the order of activities, decisions and conditions, alternative paths, repeated operations (loops), events that change the
flow, and the start and end of a process. It does not simply list the activities — it shows the possible paths through them.

 Benefit Explanation
 Understand logic step-by-step behaviour
 Identify decisions conditions such as Yes/No
 Identify alternative paths what happens when conditions differ
 Identify loops repeated operations
 Detect missing cases situations not handled
 Support testing identifies test paths
 Support design basis for program logic
 Improve communication customers, analysts and developers understand it


 Element Meaning Example
 Sequence activities one after another Login → Select Product → Add to Cart → Checkout
 Decision a condition selects one of the paths Payment successful? Yes/No
 Branching flow splits into different paths User type? Admin → Admin Panel; Customer → Home Page
 Merging different paths come together Cash / Online → Order Confirmed
 Loop operation repeated while a condition holds Enter Password → Correct? No → Try Again → back
 Parallel flow independent activities at the same time after Order Confirmed: Send Email ∥ Update Order


Control Flow Graph (CFG)
A control flow graph is the formal form: nodes = activities or statements (processing nodes and decision nodes), edges = flow of
control. Example: [Login] → <Valid Login?> → Yes [Dashboard] / No [Retry] → both lead to End.

5.3.1 Data-centered architecture

 A data store (file or database) resides at the centre; other components (clients) access it frequently to update, add, delete or
 modify data. Components communicate only through the shared repository. A variation is the blackboard: the repository
 notifies client software when data of interest changes, so data can be passed among clients. This style promotes integrability:
 existing components can be changed and new clients added without the permission or concern of other clients.


 Advantages (lecture) Disadvantages (lecture)
 centralised data · easy sharing · consistent data central repository can become a bottleneck · repository failure affects many
 management · easy to add new clients components · changes to the repository (its format) may affect several components

5.3.2 Data-flow architecture (pipe-and-filter)

 Used when input data is transformed into output data through a series of computational components. In pipe-and-filter the
 components are filters (each performs a transformation, works independently, takes input of one form and produces output of
 a specified form, and needs no knowledge of neighbouring filters) connected by pipes (transmit data from one filter to the
 next). If the flow degenerates into a single line of transforms it is called batch sequential: it accepts a batch of data and
 applies a series of sequential components to it.


 Advantages (lecture) Disadvantages (lecture)
 encourages upkeep, repurposing and modification (filters can frequently degenerates to batch sequential · does not suit applications
 be replaced or reused) · supports concurrent execution (filters needing greater user interaction · hard to coordinate two different but
 run in parallel) related streams

 1. Place the user in control. The user should feel that the system responds to them. Define interaction modes so that the user is
 not forced into unnecessary actions; give flexible interaction (keyboard / mouse); make interaction interruptible and undoable;
 hide technical internals; allow customisation; allow direct manipulation. Example: while ordering food the user can go back,
 cancel, pause and resume, and undo the removal of a dish.

 2. Reduce the user's memory load. The more the user must remember, the more error-prone the interaction. Reduce demand
 on short-term memory (show what has been chosen), set meaningful defaults, provide shortcuts, use a real-world metaphor for
 the layout, disclose information progressively. Example: the checkout shows the cart, the default address and last payment
 mode, so the user recognises instead of recalling.

 3. Make the interface consistent. Keep the task in context, keep consistency across the application family, and do not change
 established behaviour without a compelling reason. Example: every screen has the same header, back arrow top-left and OK /
 Cancel in the same order; a swipe always gives the same result.

 Q. Discuss the importance of consistency in interface design compared with placing the user in control and reducing memory
 load. Which rule has the greatest impact on user experience? Give real-world examples.

 Answer.
 The three golden-rule groups serve different goals: control gives the user power and safety, reduced memory load makes the
 interface easy to use, and consistency makes it learnable and predictable.

 Rule group What it protects If ignored Real-world example
 Place user in freedom, safety, user feels trapped, fears errors Gmail 'Undo send'; cancel any download
 control confidence
 Reduce memory efficiency, fewer user forgets, mistakes, abandons browser autofill, recent searches, saved cards
 load errors
 Consistency learnability, every screen must be learned again, same icons and gestures in all Google /
 predictability, trust mistakes from false expectations Microsoft apps; back button always top-left


 Importance of consistency. Once a user learns one part, consistency lets them transfer that knowledge to every other part; this
 itself reduces memory load (nothing new to remember) and gives control (the user can predict results). Consistency is cheap to
 apply across a product and is the basis of a family of applications; it is a precondition of the other two rules, whereas control and
 memory features add on top.

 Which has the greatest impact? It depends on the user and system. For a new or occasional user memory load matters most
 (recognition, defaults). For safety-critical or expert use control (undo, interrupt) matters most. For a large product or product
 family consistency matters most because it multiplies across all screens. A balanced judgement: consistency has the broadest
 and most lasting impact since it reduces both learning effort and memory load, but no rule can be dropped: a consistent
 interface that traps the user or hides everything behind memorised commands is still poor.

 Example of conflict: a mobile app that moves 'Back' to different corners on different screens is inconsistent even though each
 screen alone lets the user cancel; users fail because their expectation is broken.

 A testing strategy is a roadmap that tells the team what steps to perform, when they are planned and carried out, and how
 much effort, time and resources they need. It integrates test-case design techniques into a well-planned series of steps that
 result in the successful construction of the software. (Pressman Ch. 17) Testing is the process of executing a program with the
 intent of finding errors.

7.3 Integration Testing

 Integration testing is a systematic technique for constructing the software architecture while at the same time conducting
 tests to uncover errors associated with interfacing. The objective is to take unit-tested components and build a program
 structure that has been dictated by design. (Pressman 17.4)

7.4 Validation Testing and System Testing

Validation testing
Validation succeeds when the software functions in a manner that can be reasonably expected by the customer (as given in the
SRS). A test plan lists tests that check all functional requirements, behavioural characteristics, content, performance and
documentation. Alpha test: conducted at the developer's site by representative users, in a controlled setting, with the developer
recording errors. Beta test: conducted at the customer's sites by end users, in a real environment without the developer present;
users report problems. Acceptance test: formal test by the customer to decide whether to accept the system.

System testing

 7.8 SQA Activities

 Software quality assurance (SQA) is an umbrella activity, applied throughout the software process: a 'planned and systematic
 pattern of actions' that ensures high quality. It encompasses: (1) an SQA process, (2) specific QA and quality-control tasks
 (technical reviews and a multi-tiered testing strategy), (3) effective software engineering practice (methods and tools), (4)
 control of all work products and changes, (5) a procedure to ensure compliance with standards, (6) measurement and
 reporting mechanisms.


Elements (concerns) of SQA

 Element What SQA does
 Standards ensure that adopted standards (IEEE, ISO) are followed and all work products conform
 Reviews and audits technical reviews uncover errors; audits by SQA staff check that quality guidelines are followed
 Testing ensure testing is properly planned and efficiently conducted so it has the best chance of finding errors
 Error / defect collection and collect and analyse error data to learn how errors are introduced and which activities remove them
 analysis best
 Change management ensure adequate change-control practices exist, since uncontrolled change causes confusion and poor
 quality
 Education lead software process improvement and training of engineers and managers
 Vendor management set quality practices and contract mandates for bought-in or contracted software
 Security management ensure appropriate process and technology for software security
 Safety assess the impact of software failure in safety-critical systems and reduce risk
 Risk management ensure risk-management activities are conducted and contingency plans exist


SQA tasks (performed by the independent SQA group)
 1. Prepares an SQA plan for the project (evaluations, audits and reviews, standards, error reporting and tracking procedures, SQA
 work products, feedback).
 2. Participates in developing the project's software process description and reviews it for compliance with policy and standards
 (e.g. ISO 9001).

 3. Reviews software engineering activities to verify compliance with the defined process; documents and tracks deviations.
 4. Audits designated work products to verify compliance with the defined process; reports results to the project manager.

 5. Ensures that deviations in the work and work products are documented and handled according to a documented procedure.
 6. Records any noncompliance and reports it to senior management; noncompliance items are tracked until resolved.

 Spiral Boehm; risk-driven; 4 quadrants (objectives · risk analysis · develop · review & plan); loops not

 ASD Highsmith; Speculate → Collaborate → Learn; adaptive, JAD, learning-driven; uncertain

 Scrum Roles: PO, SM, Developers. Artifacts: Product backlog, Sprint backlog, Increment. Events: Sprint
